tables.heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Nicotine Use > Smoking cessation approach
tables.caption: Smoking cessation approach in clinical practice (flowchart, with nicotine dependence table)
tables.content:
All smokers should be identified and their readiness to quit evaluated. If resistance to quitting exists, information and suitable follow-up should be provided. If the person is ready to make a quit attempt, evaluation of nicotine dependence, co-morbid and psychosocial factors should guide the choice of effective interventions.

1. Ask: do you smoke? do you know the risks? have you thought of quitting?
2. Alert: do you know the benefits of quitting? do you know that we can help you?
3. Assess: are you ready to quit?
4. Assist/arrange:
   - No or maybe: give a motivational pamphlet and encourage follow-up; return to Ask at the next visit.
   - Yes: arrange for cessation intervention.
5. Specific nicotine dependence review: Fagerstrom/CO levels; current smoking and history of quit attempts; social stressors/household smokers.
   Dependence level (already attempted to quit / cigarettes per day / time to first cigarette after waking):
   - Very high: yes / >30 / >5 min (printed)
   - High: yes / 20-30 / 5-30 min
   - Medium: yes / 10-20 / 30-60 min
   - Low: no / <10 / >60 min
6. By dependence:
   - Motivated, low dependence: could manage with counselling/support alone or NRT; support group, text/internet/smartphone-based support.
   - Motivated, high dependence: probably will need added pharmacological support; assess medical/psychiatric history; evaluate capacity to purchase medicine; review availability of medication. Medication options: nicotine replacement therapy (patch/gum/spray), varenicline, bupropion.
7. Set quit date: arrange appropriate support and medication if needed.
8. Follow-up: assess withdrawal symptoms and drug side-effects; evaluate mood and psychosocial stressors; identify potential for relapse.

CO = carbon monoxide; NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.

tables.caption: Key messages for patients about alcohol
tables.content:
- NO amount of alcohol is safe for your health.
- The safest choice is NOT to drink alcohol at all.
- Alcohol increases your risk of cancer, heart disease, liver disease, and many other conditions.
- Quitting alcohol improves your health at any age.
- You don't have to quit alone: ask for help from healthcare providers, family, and support groups.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Hypertension > Algorithm for hypertension screening
tables.caption: Algorithm for hypertension screening in adults (18 years and above)
tables.content:
Adults (18 years and above), by office blood pressure:
- Optimal <120/80: repeat at least every 5 years.
- Normal 120-129/80-84: repeat at least every 3 years.
- High normal BP 130-139/85-89: consider masked hypertension; repeat annually. Consider out-of-office measurements (ABPM or HBPM).
- Hypertension >140/90: repeated visits for office BP measurement, and consider out-of-office measurements (ABPM or HBPM).

Adopted from ESC/ESH guidelines, 2023.
N.B.: the Ministry of Health recommends measuring blood pressure yearly for adults ≥18 years of age.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Diabetes Mellitus > Algorithm for diabetes mellitus screening
tables.caption: Algorithm for diabetes mellitus screening in adults
tables.content:
All clients >18 years attending a health facility should be screened for diabetes using the known risk factors below.
- No risk factors: re-evaluate.
- Risk factors present: test (HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, oral glucose tolerance test, or random glucose):
  - HbA1c <5.7% / FPG <100 mg/dl: encourage healthy lifestyle maintenance; retest at least annually.
  - HbA1c 5.6-6.4% / FPG 100-125 mg/dl / OGTT 140-199 mg/dl: encourage lifestyle modification and retest every 6-12 months.
  - HbA1c ≥ 6.5% / FPG ≥ 126 mg/dl: retest with a different test, and refer for treatment if still positive.

*Known risk factors for diabetes: physical inactivity; family history of diabetes; high-risk race or ethnicity (African, Indian); hypertension (≥ 140/90); HDL-C <35 or triglyceride > 250 mg/dL; history of gestational diabetes or gave birth to a baby ≥4.5 kg; history of heart disease; conditions associated with insulin resistance; polycystic ovary syndrome; malnutrition.

Adapted from the American Diabetes Association Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes. N.B.: the Ministry of Health recommends measuring glycaemia yearly in adults ≥ 18 years of age.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Chronic Kidney Disease > CKD clinical protocol (kidney health check)
tables.caption: Chronic kidney disease clinical protocol: kidney health check, confirmation and staging
tables.content:
Offer a kidney health check to people with: diabetes; hypertension; established CVD; family history of kidney failure; obesity (BMI ≥30); current or past smoker/vaper; history of AKI aged ≥60 years; high index of suspicion in clients, especially paediatrics, with oedema and recurrent puffiness.

Tests: uACR, eGFR, and trace protein on urine dipstick.
- uACR ≥3 mg/mmol (yes): repeat uACR within 3 months. If uACR normal, complete a third test (preferably first morning void). CKD if a minimum of two uACRs ≥3 mg/mmol over 3 months.
- eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m2 (yes): repeat eGFR within 7 days; if ≥20% reduction in eGFR, possible AKI: discuss with nephrologist. Repeat eGFR within 3 months. CKD if a minimum of two eGFRs <60 mL/min/1.73m2 over 3 months.
- No to both: repeat kidney health check (annually if aged ≥18, people with diabetes or hypertension).
If either (and/or) criterion is met: stage CKD with the staging table, using eGFR and uACR results.
source_flags: The 'two eGFRs <60 over 3 months' window is implied by the 3-month repeat; the PDF box reads 'If minimum of two eGFRs <60mL/min.1.73m2'.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Lipids Disorders > Lipid management clinical decision pathway
tables.caption: Lipid management: clinical decision pathway (CV risk, comorbidities, lipid targets)
tables.content:
Obtain fasting lipids at baseline and annually. Then three parallel assessments, then treat to the target:
1. Calculate and categorize CV risk using the Framingham risk score (mdcalc.com - Framingham Risk Score). Risk categories: low risk < 10%; moderate risk 10%-19%; high risk > 20%.
2. Assess comorbidities: diabetes; CAD; previous CV event; atherosclerosis; aneurysm. *Any = high risk.
3. Determine lipid targets:
   - LDL-C: optimal <100 mg/dL; near or above optimal 100-129 mg/dL; borderline high 130-159 mg/dL; high 160-189 mg/dL; very high ≥190 mg/dL.
   - Total cholesterol: desirable <200 mg/dL; borderline high 200-239 mg/dL; high ≥240 mg/dL.
   - Triglycerides: normal <150 mg/dL; borderline high ≥150-199 mg/dL; high 200-499 mg/dL; very high ≥500 mg/dL.
Then: treat to the target.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Chronic Kidney Disease > Algorithm for CKD screening
tables.caption: Algorithm for chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening
tables.content:
Target population:
- No markers of risk: do not screen.
- Risk factors (high blood pressure, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, family history, HIV): screen.

Screen: test (urine dipstick, blood glucose, blood pressure, family history) and measure kidney function (serum creatinine; estimate the eGFR).
Determine if test results indicate CKD (eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 or presence of albuminuria):
- No: rescreen based on the risks.
- Yes: lifestyle modification (smoking cessation; balanced diet; regular exercise; limit salt intake to <2 g/day); medical treatment (diabetes, BP and lipid control: SGLT2, ACEI/ARB, statins, metformin...); considerations (drug dosing; use of contrast media; CKD complications: anaemia, hyperkalaemia, bone disease, CVD...).
Then: retesting; follow-up visits; referral to nephrology when appropriate.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes > Definition, classification and treatment targets
tables.caption: Diabetes mellitus: definition, classification and treatment targets

body.t: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic condition in which the pancreas no longer produces enough insulin (impaired insulin secretion) or cells stop responding to the insulin that is produced (insulin resistance), resulting in increased blood glucose.

1. Type 1 diabetes: due to autoimmune b-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood. 2. Type 2 diabetes: due to a progressive loss of b-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance.

Monogenic diabetes syndromes (neonatal diabetes; maturity-onset diabetes of the young). Diseases of the exocrine pancreas (such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatitis). Drug- or chemical-induced diabetes: glucocorticoid use, treatment of HIV/AIDS, or after organ transplantation. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): diabetes diagnosed in the second or third trimester of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes before gestation.
HbA1c <7% for most adults. HbA1c <6.5% for type 1 diabetes without hypoglycaemia. HbA1c <8% for people with frequent hypoglycaemia, limited life expectancy, or cardiovascular complications.
All clients on treatment should aim for a glycaemia (random or fasting) ranging 5-10 mmol/L.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Type 2 diabetes pharmacological treatment
tables.caption: Type 2 diabetes pharmacological treatment (flowchart, by HbA1c)
tables.content:
Newly diagnosed type 2 DM patient: check HbA1c. Health promotion for all (disease, medication adherence, nutrition, behaviour), individual and group.

By HbA1c at diagnosis:
- HbA1c <7%: lifestyle modification; recheck HbA1c in 6 months.
- HbA1c 7-8% (printed '<7%-8%'): start metformin [note 1]: 1. 500 mg OD; 2. recheck HbA1c in 3 months; 3. increase dose every 3 months until at goal or maximum tolerated dose.
- HbA1c 8-9.9% (printed '<8%-9.9%'): consider dual therapy: 1. start metformin 500 mg OD and titrate every 2 weeks to a maximum of 2 g if tolerated; 2. add a second drug (sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors).
- HbA1c >10%: consider insulin: consider starting the patient on insulin therapy alone or in combination with metformin (consult physician). Start at low-dose insulin and increase until target reached.

Follow-up after lifestyle modification or metformin:
- HbA1c <7%: 1. continue current medication; 2. recheck HbA1c in 6 months; 3. fasting blood glucose every 3 months.
- HbA1c >7%: 1. add a second OGLA, e.g. sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors; 2. recheck HbA1c in 3 months; 3. increase the dose of the second agent until glycaemic target reached, or maximum dose. If HbA1c remains >8%, review with physician and consider referral to the diabetes clinic for insulin management.

T2DM diagnosis criteria: 1. FPG > 7.0 mmol/L; 2. random glucose > 11.1 mmol/L; 3. need two positive tests, one must be FBG.
For older patients, it is reasonable to set the HbA1c goal at < 8%.

[note 1] Caution: metformin use in patients with reduced kidney function: 1. do not start new patients on metformin if CrCl < 45 ml/min; 2. continue metformin if already on it and CrCl is 30-45 ml/min, but repeat CrCl in 6 months; 3. stop metformin if CrCl < 30 ml/min.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Pharmacotherapy progression in type 2 diabetes
tables.caption: Pharmacotherapy progression in type 2 diabetes (monotherapy to triple therapy and insulin)

body.t: Metformin is the drug of first choice at diagnosis.

Continue until contraindicated or not tolerated. If metformin is contraindicated or not tolerated, use gliclazide. For patients with established cardiovascular disease intolerant to metformin, consider SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1RA (under specialist care).
Consider if the patient has symptomatic hyperglycaemia and HbA1c >9% at diagnosis. Review gliclazide continuation once metformin dose and lifestyle interventions are optimized.
Add a second agent if target not achieved with monotherapy

Options to add: gliclazide, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, or SGLT2 inhibitor. Consider comorbidities, ability to access medicines, and properties of each drug. Fixed-dose combinations (e.g., DPP-4 inhibitor + metformin) may offer compliance and cost advantages.
Add a third oral agent or an injectable agent

Consider if HbA1c is above individualized target (typically <7% for most) with two oral agents. Injectable options: GLP-1RA or basal insulin. Do NOT combine: GLP-1RA with DPP-4 inhibitor; GLP-1RA with SGLT2 inhibitor; pioglitazone with insulin.
Add a third oral agent or an injectable agent.
For patients on three oral agents who are still not at target. Other oral agents can be stopped upon initiation of premix insulin.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes > Indications and timing for insulin
tables.caption: Insulin therapy in type 2 diabetes: indications, when to initiate, and good practice

body.t: Poor glycaemic control: HbA1c still [above target] despite previous attempts to improve with lifestyle modification and maximum oral therapy. Patient is symptomatic (weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia, recurrent infections). Steroid-induced diabetes. Patient unable to tolerate or has contraindication to OGLAs. Gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy not controlled on OGLAs. Painful neuropathy. Foot ulceration and infection.

As soon as there is evidence of sub-optimal glycaemic control. After reviewing the patient's ability to change their lifestyle and medication concordance. Following a full discussion with the patient that includes identifying barriers to insulin initiation, e.g. occupational issues, fear of weight gain, fear of hypoglycaemia and fear of injections.

Insulin initiation should be part of a structured educational programme for the patient, and competent health care staff should have sufficient time for initiation and follow-up until glycaemic control is optimized. The decision to start insulin should be made in partnership with the person, and the choice of regimen should cater for individual needs. The person initiating insulin should be trained and competent to do so in line with the national guidelines, and should consult with the physician/diabetologist. Ensure educational materials and support literature are available for the patient starting insulin. Patients requiring insulin prior to pregnancy should be referred to the gynaecologist.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes > Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM
tables.caption: Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM (flowchart)
tables.content:
Steps run from 1 injection (more flexible, lower patient complexity) to 3+ injections (less flexible, high complexity).

Step 1 - Basal insulin (usually with metformin), 1 injection:
  Start: 10 units per day, or 0.1 to 0.2 units per kg per day.
  Adjust: 10% to 15%, or 2 to 4 units, once or twice weekly to reach fasting BG target.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 4 units or 10% to 20%.

If not controlled after fasting BG target is reached (or if dose > 0.5 units per kg per day), treat postprandial glucose excursions with mealtime insulin (consider an initial glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist trial). Two options (2 injections, moderate complexity):

Option A - Add 1 rapid-acting insulin injection before the largest meal:
  Start: 4 units, 0.1 units per kg, or 10% of basal dose; if A1C <8%, consider decreasing basal insulin by the same amount.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
  If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).

Option B - Change to premixed insulin twice daily:
  Start: divide current basal dose into 2/3 a.m. and 1/3 p.m., or into 1/2 a.m. and 1/2 p.m.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
  If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).

Step 3 - Add 2 or more rapid-acting insulin injections before the largest meals (basal-bolus, 3+ injections, high complexity):
  Start: 4 units, 0.1 units per kg, or 10% of basal dose per meal; if A1C < 8%, consider decreasing basal dose by the same amount.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.

NB: for clients already on a single injectable agent, e.g. basal insulin, consider escalation to any of: 1. combination basal insulin and GLP-1RA therapy; 2. premix (twice daily) insulin; 3. basal-plus insulin therapy (adding one or more prandial doses of insulin to basal insulin). For all three options, metformin should be retained; consider stopping the other oral agents to reduce the cost and complexity of the regimen.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 1 Diabetes > Diagnosis of T1DM
tables.caption: Diagnosis of type 1 diabetes (T1DM)
tables.content:
Three stages, shown as three boxes:
1. Symptoms (loss of weight, polyuria, polydipsia, ...): increased risk of diabetes. Suspect diabetes.
2. Symptoms + glucose criteria: in case of abnormal plasma glucose values, experts suggest getting an HbA1c as a useful baseline. Diabetes is confirmed by: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dl); random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dl); HbA1c ≥ 6.5%. Immune-mediated diabetes: presence of autoimmune markers.
3. Immune-mediated diabetes (in tertiary care): presence of autoimmune markers: islet cell autoantibodies and autoantibodies to GAD (GAD65), insulin, the tyrosine phosphatases IA-2 and IA-2β, and ZnT8.

tables.context_before: Basal-bolus regimen (preferred regimen): short acting insulin 15-30 minutes before a meal, or rapid acting insulin with main meals (e.g. breakfast, lunch and main evening meal); intermediate acting insulin before bed. tables.table_note: OR three injections daily: a mixture of short and intermediate acting (premixed 70:30) insulin before breakfast; short acting insulin alone before an afternoon snack or main evening meal; intermediate acting insulin before bed (or variations). OR two injections daily: a mixture (premixed combination) of short and intermediate acting insulins before breakfast and the main evening meal. The total daily dose is divided so that 2/3 is given in the morning and 1/3 in the evening; each dose is split between intermediate-acting and short-acting insulin in a 70:30 ratio (pre-mixed). tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Diabetes Emergencies > Diagnosis, monitoring, resolution and subcutaneous insulin protocol
tables.caption: Management of diabetic emergencies (DKA and HHS): diagnosis, evaluation, monitoring, resolution, transition to SC insulin, alternative SC insulin protocol and formulas

body.t: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) are two of the most serious acute complications of diabetes. DKA is characterized by ketoacidosis and hyperglycemia, while HHS usually has more severe hyperglycemia without ketoacidosis.
Based on clinical evaluation and immediate bedside investigations. Features include polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, abdominal pain, fruity odor, confusion, Kussmaul breathing, dehydration.

Hyperglycemia: BG >13.9 mmol/L. Euglycemia <250 mg/dl (pregnancy, SGLT2 use). Ketonuria or ketonemia (>3 mmol/L): highly positive. Acidosis: pH <7.3, low HCO3- (printed ':<10 ≤ 15 mEq/L'). Anion gap: >12 (see formula).
Severe hyperglycemia: BG (printed '>600>1000 mg/dl 33.3 mmol/L'). Hyperosmolality: effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg (see formula). Neurologic signs: focal signs, obtundation, seizure, coma.

Vital signs, volume status (decreased skin turgor, dry axillae and oral mucosa, low JVP, tachycardia and hypotension), mental status. Immediately: serum blood glucose, urine ketones. Additional testing: FBC, electrolytes, FT, ABG. Evaluate for precipitating causes: septic screen (urinalysis, blood cultures), cardiac enzymes, ECG, CXR. Pregnancy test if indicated.

BG hourly. Urinary ketones and serum pH for DKA, and serum osmolality for HHS, 4-hourly. Electrolytes, primarily Na+ and K+, 4-hourly. Mental status: expect improvement with treatment if DKA or HHS are the causes; consider further evaluation if not improving. Input/output, hydration status; vital signs hourly.
BG < 15 mmol/L + 2 or more of: HCO3- ≥ 15 mEq/L; pH > 7.3; anion gap ≤ 12 mEq/L. Negative urine ketones if the above are not available (confirm with repeat in 1-2 hrs).
BG < [value missing in source]; improved mental status; effective osmolality ≤ 315 mOsm/kg.

Continue continuous IV for 1-2 hrs after long-acting insulin is started. 0.4-0.6 u/kg for insulin-naive patients. NPH/regular: based on inpatient DM protocol. Hold regular insulin if patient is not eating. May resume home regimen if previously on insulin.

This regimen is not well validated and is modified from other protocols; continuous IV is preferred as standard of care when available. If continuous infusion is not available, for mild/moderate DKA: initial IV bolus 0.1 IU/kg given intravenously; maintenance 0.1 IU/kg subcutaneous every 1-2 hours (start immediately following the bolus). When BG <250 mg/dL, reduce dose by 50%. Continue until resolution of DKA or HHS.

Calculated anion gap (>12 is elevated) = [Na+] − [Cl- + HCO3-]. Effective serum osmolality = 2x[Na+K] + urea + glucose (usually <330 mosmol/kg in DKA and > 350 mosmol/kg in HHS). Corrected serum sodium = [Na+] + 1.6 x [glucose (mg/dL) − 100]/100. Free water deficit = 0.6 x weight (kg) x [(Na+/140) − 1].

Step 3: target glucose reduction 3-4 mmol/L/hr. Target BGL 10-15 mmol/L. NEVER drop >5 mmol/L/hr.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for DKA
tables.caption: Algorithm for DKA (flowchart: assessment, resuscitation, IV therapy, insulin, monitoring, cerebral oedema)
tables.content:
Immediate assessment:
- Clinical history: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, enuresis, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, fatigue, confusion, level of consciousness.
- Clinical signs: dehydration; deep sighing respiration (Kussmaul); smell of ketones; lethargy/drowsiness.
- Biochemical features & investigations: ketones in urine; blood glucose; acidaemia (vpH < 7.3, HCO3 <15 mmol/L); urea, electrolytes; other investigations as indicated.
Diagnosis confirmed: diabetic ketoacidosis. Contact senior staff.

Then by clinical state:
A. Shock (reduced peripheral pulses), reduced conscious level/coma: resuscitation: airway ± NG tube; breathing (100% oxygen); circulation: 0.9% saline 10-20 ml/kg over 1-2 h, repeat until circulation is restored (see CE management). Then IV therapy (as B).
B. Dehydration >5%, not in shock, acidotic (hyperventilation), vomiting: IV therapy: saline 0.9% 10 ml/kg over 1 h, may repeat; calculate fluid requirements; correct fluid deficit over 24-48 hours; ECG for abnormal T-waves; add KCl 40 mmol per litre of fluid.
C. Minimal dehydration, tolerating oral fluid: therapy: start with SC insulin; continue oral hydration. If no improvement: IV therapy (as B).

After IV therapy: continuous insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hour, starting 1 hour after fluids initiated.

Critical observations: hourly blood glucose; hourly fluid input & output; neurological status at least hourly; electrolytes 2-hourly after starting IV fluid therapy; monitor ECG for T-wave changes.

Then:
- Acidosis not improving: re-evaluate IV fluid calculations, insulin delivery system & dose, need for additional resuscitation; consider sepsis.
- Blood glucose ≤17 mmol/L (300 mg/dL) or blood glucose falls >5 mmol/L/hour (90 mg/dL): IV therapy: change to 0.45% or 0.9% saline; add glucose to fluids (5%-12.5%) to prevent hypoglycaemia; adjust sodium infusion to promote an increase in measured serum sodium. When improved (clinically well, ketoacidosis resolved, tolerating oral fluids): transition to SC insulin: start SC insulin, then stop IV insulin after an appropriate interval.
- Neurological deterioration: warning signs: severe or progressive headache, slowing heart rate, irritability, confusion, decreased consciousness, incontinence, specific neurological signs. Exclude hypoglycaemia; is it cerebral oedema? CE (cerebral oedema) management: give mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg or 3% hypertonic saline; adjust IV fluids to maintain normal BP but avoid over-hydration; call senior staff; move to ICU; consider cranial imaging only after the patient is stabilized.

tables.caption: Subcutaneous insulin order protocol (basal, bolus and correction) for adult non-ICU patients who are NPO, on TPN, eating or tube-fed

body.t: For adult patients who are NPO*, on TPN**, eating meals, or on bolus or continuous tube feedings. Not used for ICU patients, DKA, or hyperosmolar state. Initiate the protocol for adult patients with known diabetes mellitus and anyone with two or more random (e.g., 6 hours apart) blood glucose readings > 10 mmol/l (order HbA1c if none obtained).

To minimize the need for correction insulin doses (sliding scale) and to provide insulin as regularly scheduled basal and bolus insulin for more efficient control of blood glucose. To maintain capillary blood glucose (CBG) at 7.8-10.0 mmol/L.

Measure CBG: eating patients: before meals and at bedtime; bolus tube-feeding patients: before each feeding; NPO or continuous tube-feeding patients: every 4 hours (rapid insulin) or every 6 hours (regular insulin). In case of high morning blood sugar, measure CBG at 3:00 a.m. to distinguish between Somogyi effect and dawn phenomenon.

Discontinue all previous antihyperglycemic agents (injection/oral): yes/no; if yes, continue to calculate the insulin dose. Calculate the initial total daily insulin (TDI) per day: 0.25 units per kg: chronic kidney disease not on dialysis; 0.3 units per kg: underweight (BMI < 18.5), older age (≥65 years), haemodialysis; 0.4 units per kg: normal weight (BMI 18.5-24.9); 0.5 units per kg: overweight (BMI 25.0-29.9); ≥ 0.6 units per kg: obese (BMI ≥30), glucocorticoids, insulin resistance.
Order 50% of the TDI. Should be given even if NPO*. Reduce dose by 25% if NPO*/poor intake/glycaemia well controlled. ___ units subcutaneous at ___ (Q24 or Q12 hours).

Order 50% of the TDI. HOLD if NPO*, TPN**, low oral intake. Divided equally before each meal/bolus feed. If continuous feed: every 4 hours (rapid insulin), every 6 hours (regular insulin). Insulin REGULAR: ___ units SC 30 minutes BEFORE each meal/bolus feed, or every 6 hours if continuous feed.

SHOULD be ordered and given even if NPO*. Eating patients: before meals and at bedtime (prefer rapid acting insulin); insulin REGULAR SC 30 minutes before meals. Bolus feed patients: before each feeding. TPN**, NPO* or continuous tube feeding: every 4 hours (rapid acting insulin), every 6 hours (regular insulin).

tables.caption: Chronic microvascular complications of diabetes (nephropathy, eye disease, neuropathy): who to screen, how, management and referral criteria

body.t: Type 1 diabetes: duration > 5 years. Type 2 diabetes: at diagnosis.

Yearly check for proteinuria (reagent strips); if positive, exclude/treat UTIs, then refer if persistent. Yearly check for microalbuminuria (reagent strips or ACR). Measure serum creatinine bi-annually.

Optimize glycaemic control (with caution in advanced disease). Aggressive BP control (<125/75 mmHg). Use ACEI or ARBs as first-line (contraindicated in pregnancy). Stop tobacco use. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides). Metformin should not be used if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2.

Type 2 diabetes: at presentation. Type 1 diabetes: >5 years duration (or at presentation if uncontrolled).

Full eye examination including visual acuity and fundoscopy (preferably dilated) at initial contact; refer if no capacity. Repeat examinations annually, or more frequently if retinopathy is progressing. Women planning pregnancy and during the first trimester require a comprehensive exam. Type 1 pregnant women: fundoscopy every trimester.
Intensify management of blood pressure, glycaemia, and lipids. Stop smoking. Patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy should avoid weight-bearing exercises and require guided exercises.

Sudden deterioration of vision. 'Floater' sensation reported by patient. Fundoscopy findings of dot or blot haemorrhages 1 disc-width away from the macula. Cataract present. Proliferative or exudative retinopathy.
Not specified as a screening criterion, but assessment is part of clinical care.

Detailed history (numbness, tingling, pain). Examination of the feet: test sensation using 10 g monofilament, 128 Hz tuning fork, or cotton wool. Lying-and-standing BP and pulse rate to check for postural hypotension.
Improve glycaemic control. Exclude or treat other contributory factors (e.g., alcohol, B12 deficiency, smoking, HIV). Symptomatic treatment (see peripheral neuropathy guidelines).
Referral to secondary and/or tertiary centre once symptomatic peripheral neuropathy is diagnosed.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes > Diabetes in Pregnancy > GDM screening, risk factors, management, complications and preconception plan
tables.caption: Gestational diabetes (GDM): screening, risk factors, management, glycaemic goals, complications and preconception plan

body.t: Universal screening (every pregnant woman) is recommended. If the woman has more than one risk factor, do an RBS/FBS at first contact. Screening should be done at 24-28 weeks (or at first contact if the patient presents late). Perform a 75 g OGTT: administer 75 g of glucose orally after an 8-hr overnight fast and measure blood glucose after 1 hour and 2 hours (1 standard level teaspoon = 5 g).

Previous GDM; maternal age > 35 years; family history of diabetes (first-degree relative); obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m2); previous macrosomia (birthweight > 4000 g); polycystic ovary syndrome; iatrogenic: glucocorticoids and antipsychotic medication; hypertension.

Intermediate hyperglycaemia or impaired glucose tolerance: HbA1c ≥ 5.7%, impaired glucose tolerance or impaired fasting glucose. HbA1c >6.5%: diagnosis of pre-existing diabetes. Note: symptoms may be non-specific.
Exercise 30-60 min moderate intensity. Diet: regular meal plan; 3 moderate-sized meals, 4 snacks; low sugar. Pharmacotherapy: see the GDM pharmacotherapy dosing schedule.

Fasting and pre-prandial blood glucose <95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L). One-hour postprandial <140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). Two-hour postprandial <120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L). Check HbA1c every 4-6 weeks; goal below 6.5%.

Maternal-neonatal: preeclampsia; gestational hypertension; hydramnios; urinary tract/vaginal infections; caesarean delivery; traumatic labour/perineal tears; postpartum haemorrhage; difficulty initiating and/or maintaining breastfeeding.

Fetal: stillbirth or neonatal death; preterm birth; congenital malformations; macrosomia; cardiomyopathy; birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, bone fracture or brachial plexus injury); hypoglycaemia; hyperbilirubinaemia; respiratory distress syndrome.

Maternal-neonatal: recurrence of GDM; type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension; ischaemic heart disease; non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; dyslipidaemia; chronic kidney disease; metabolic syndrome; hyperinsulinaemia.

Fetal: childhood obesity; excess abdominal adiposity; higher blood pressure; possible earlier-onset cardiovascular disease; possible attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder; autism spectrum disorder.

Optimize modifiable risk factors (e.g. BMI, diet, physical activity). Screen glycaemia in high-risk women. For pre-existing DM: maintain HbA1c below 6% with appropriate drugs (insulin and metformin). Screen for complications.

Healthy diet and regular exercise unless there are obstetric contraindications. Possible personalized gestational weight gain. High-risk women: detect early DM in pregnancy (if preconception screening positive). Follow the protocol for all at 24-28 weeks according to recommended screening and diagnostic criteria. Delivery at 38 weeks is advised if sugars are well controlled; if poorly controlled, consult a specialist on timing of delivery. Consider steroids for lung maturation if early delivery is indicated. If steroids are given at any point in pregnancy, anticipate difficult glycaemic control; insulin therapy is advised. Aim for blood glucose 4-7 mmol/L during active labour and delivery. Anticipate maternal and fetal/neonatal complications at delivery and plan for necessary interventions.

Early postpartum OGTT to assess glucose status. Regular long-term follow-up focused on diabetes and cardiovascular risk factor modification. Family lifestyle support: optimizing diet, physical activity, and weight in the offspring.

tables.caption: Diabetic emergencies (DKA/HHS) in special populations: HIV/TB co-infection, resource-limited settings, pregnancy, elderly

body.t: Screen for HIV if status unknown (rapid test on admission). Immune reconstitution can unmask T1DM. ARVs (especially older PI-based) can cause insulin resistance. Opportunistic infections (PCP, cryptococcal, TB) are common DKA precipitants. Maintain ARTs during crisis; liaise with HIV team.

No blood ketones: use urine ketones (≥2+ = significant). No VBG: treat on clinical picture + glucose + ketones. No syringe pump: 50 units in 500 ml NS (0.1 unit/ml) + drip control. No 0.45% NaCl: use 0.9% NaCl throughout with closer monitoring. Validate POC glucose meters for high glucose ranges >30 mmol/L.

DKA can occur at lower glucose (euglycaemic DKA in pregnancy). Involve obstetric team immediately. Fetal monitoring from 24 weeks onwards. Higher insulin requirements: do not underdose. Avoid bicarbonate unless pH <7.0.

Reduced physiological reserve: higher risk of fluid overload. More gradual fluid replacement over 48-72 hours. Increased thromboembolic risk: early LMWH prophylaxis. Exclude silent MI, stroke, UTI, pneumonia as precipitant. Assess cognition, falls risk, social support before discharge.

tables.caption: Interpreting TSH and FT4/FT3 results (thyroid function test flowchart)
tables.content:
Start with TSH.

TSH low:
- FT4 and/or FT3 high (printed 'Nor FT4 and/or FT3 high'): primary hyperthyroidism. Perform test for TRAb/TSI; consider ordering thyroid scintigraphy. Repeat TFT in four weeks to determine course or impact of treatment. Specialist referral*.
- FT4 and FT3 normal*: subclinical/mild hyperthyroidism. Repeat TSH, FT4 and FT3 in 1-3 months; may require further investigation.
- FT4 and/or FT3 low: discordant: non-thyroidal illness; central hypothyroidism. Repeat TSH, FT4 and FT3 and follow to assess trend; if persistently abnormal, refer for further investigation.

TSH normal: thyroid dysfunction excluded.

TSH high:
- FT4 low: primary hypothyroidism. Repeat TSH and FT4; check anti-TPO; treat with levothyroxine.
- FT4 normal: subclinical/mild hypothyroidism. Repeat in 1-3 months; check anti-TPO antibody; monitor TFT annually if stable; consider treatment with levothyroxine*.
- FT4 high: discordant: TSHoma; thyroid hormone resistance; assay interference. Repeat TSH and FT4 to assess trend; refer for further investigation.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism > Management of thyroid storm > Recognition and management (flowchart)
tables.caption: Thyroid storm: recognition and management (flowchart)
tables.content:
1. Suspect thyroid storm (BWPS ≥45).
2. Identify precipitant(s).
3. Initial stabilization (ABC). Propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole.
4. Block thyroid hormone synthesis (≥ 1 h after ATD): Lugol's iodine 8 drops PO q6-8h, or NaI IV 0.25-0.5 g q6h.
5. Block peripheral effects: propranolol 60-80 mg OG 6-hourly, or 1 mg IV q10min (max 3); hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h.
6. Continuous monitoring & support: ECG, vitals, fluid balance, electrolytes. Adjust therapy as needed.

In addition to general supportive measures, therapy should be directed at the thyroid gland and the hypermetabolism and tachycardia. Patients should be monitored in an intensive or high care setting. The underlying precipitant should be actively treated and managed. Prevention is key: correct thyroid function before elective surgery.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism in Pregnancy > Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy
tables.caption: Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy (flowchart)
tables.content:
Two entry points:
- Known hyperthyroidism on ATD and wishing to conceive/pregnant: switch to a 'dose titration' regimen if on 'block and replace'. Use PTU pre-conception and in the 1st trimester; use CBZ (carbimazole) thereafter.
- New diagnosis of hyperthyroidism during pregnancy: commence anti-thyroid medication: PTU in the first trimester, CBZ thereafter.

Both: refer to endocrine physician. Then two parallel tracks:

Track 1 - check TFTs every 4 weeks (and LFTs every 4 weeks if on PTU):
- Free T4 above normal reference range: increase dose of ATD.
- Free T4 at or just above upper end of normal reference range: continue on current dose of ATD.
- Free T4 below upper end of normal reference range: decrease dose of ATD.
Repeat the 4-weekly checks throughout pregnancy. TFTs to be checked 6-8 weeks post-partum (printed 'at first ante-natal check').

Track 2 - check TRAb at 22 weeks and 36 weeks. If TRAb > 2-3 times the upper limit of normal: obstetric ultrasound for monitoring for fetal thyrotoxicosis.

Reference: Girling JC. Thyroid disease in pregnancy. The Obstetrician and Gynaecologist 2008; 10:237-243.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Heart Failure > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Heart Failure
tables.caption: Algorithm for diagnosis and management of heart failure (by facility level, echo availability, congestion; guideline-directed therapy and CRT)
tables.content:
1. Suspected heart failure? Take a history and examine.
   - Clinic history: symptoms (acute: raised JVD, PND, lower limb swelling); function limitation (NYHA class); prior cardiac disease, pregnancies; prior comorbidities (HTN, disease, others); drugs, toxins.
   - Physical exam: vital signs; signs of congestion (raised JVD, hepatomegaly); lower limb swelling; murmur; crackles.
2. Investigations by facility level:
   - Health Center: LABS: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, CXR, ECG. If congested with SatO2 <90%: give IV Lasix (furosemide) 40 mg and transfer to the regional hospital.
   - Regional Hospital: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, HbA1c, chest X-ray, ECG, +/- cardiac ultrasound. Refer on to the referral hospital as needed.
   - Referral Hospital: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, HbA1c, ferritin, chest X-ray, cardiac ultrasound, ECG, coronary CTA, cardiac MRI.
3. Still suspect heart failure? (at DH/PH/referral hospital) Yes → Is heart ultrasound (echo) available?
   - No: treat as HFrEF (EF ≤40%) and refer to cardiology.
   - Yes: HFrEF & HFmrEF on echo → look for cardiomyopathy or valvular heart disease.
     - Not congested: work up causes (genetics, inflammatory, toxins, pregnancy, metabolic).
4. If congested (from either path): IV Lasix (8-hourly), morphine (if no low BP), nitrates (if available), oxygen (if low SpO2).
   - Cardiogenic shock: IV inotropes/pressors, until euvolemic.
5. When euvolemic, start guideline-directed medical therapy: 1. RAASi; 2. beta-blocker; 3. MRA (EF ≤35%); 4. SGLT2i → RAASi + BB + MRA ± SGLT2i.
6. After 3 months of GDMT, if EF ≤35% plus LBBB: CRT (cardiac resynchronisation therapy).

tables.content:
Still suspect heart failure? (at HC/PH/referral hospital) → Heart ultrasound available? Yes → LVEF >50%:
- With BP >180/110 mmHg: hypertensive heart disease (HFpEF); calculate the H2FPEF score.
  - If congested: IV Lasix (8-hourly), oxygen (if low SpO2), position semi-sitting.
  - Screen for comorbidities: diabetes, dyslipidemia, AF, CAD, HTN.
  - BP control: 1. SGLT2i; 2. beta-blocker (if AF); 3. RAASi; 4. CCB.
- With mitral restricted opening, hockey-stick deformity, dilated LA on echo, and an apical diastolic murmur: mitral stenosis.
  - Causes: 1. rheumatic; 2. calcific; 3. congenital; 4. valvulitis.
  - Treat: Lasix (if congested); penicillin V (rheumatic); beta-blocker (atenolol).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Heart Failure > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Heart Failure > Valvular, right heart and pericardial disease
tables.caption: Heart failure algorithm (continued): valvular heart disease, right heart failure, pericardial disease, other diagnoses and precipitants of acute heart failure; inotrope dosing
tables.content:
Still suspect heart failure? (at HC/PH/referral hospital) → Heart ultrasound available? Yes → LVEF >50%:
- BP normal or high, valvular heart disease & CHD: 1. Lasix (if overloaded); 2. RAASi (high BP or LV remodelling); 3. +/- penicillin V; 4. cardiology consult.
  - If congested: IV Lasix (8-hourly), oxygen (if low SpO2), position semi-sitting.
- Dilated RV + D-shape sign, TAPSE <1.7 cm, loud P2: right heart failure. 1. Lasix (if congested); 2. screen for the cause of pulmonary HTN (acute/chronic lung disease, PE, other).
- Pericardial effusion: pericardial disease. 1. Pericardiocentesis (if tamponade): refer to cardiologist; 2. screen for and treat the cause: infections (TB, HIV, CMV, EBV), metabolic (thyroid disorders, uremia), malignancy, connective tissue disease; 3. others.
- Heart failure unlikely and normal heart ultrasound: consider other plausible diagnoses.

Precipitants of acute heart failure: 1. dietary indiscretion (alcohol, high salt); 2. medical non-adherence; 3. renal failure (acute/CKD progression); 4. new drugs (BB, CCB, NSAIDs, others); 5. arrhythmias, valve dysfunction; 6. new infection (pneumonia, others); 7. myocardial ischemia/infarction, PE; 8. metabolic (thyroid, DKA, pancreatitis); 9. hypertensive crisis.

Inotropes: IV dobutamine or dopamine 200 mg. Dose: 10-20 mcg/kg/min. Example for a 70 kg adult: 2 ampoules in 50 cc NS by syringe pump at 5.25-10.5 cc/h; or, if no syringe pump, 5 ampoules in 500 cc NS over 24 hours = 21 cc/h ≈ 7 drops/min. Keep MAP ≥ 65.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Ischemic Heart Disease > Approach to Patient with Chest Pain
tables.caption: Approach to the patient with chest pain (flowchart: ACS, STEMI/NSTEMI/unstable angina, pericarditis, pneumothorax, pneumonia, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism)
tables.content:
1. Initial assessment with vitals (BP, all peripheral pulses, RR, temperature, JVP, SpO2) and physical examination (CVS, respiratory system, GIS).
   - Hemodynamically unstable: stabilize and immediately assess for STEMI, aortic dissection, massive pulmonary embolism, pericardial tamponade.
   - Hemodynamically stable: evaluate the causes of chest pain.
2. Obtain a 12-lead ECG, echo and CXR (all patients).
3. ECG diagnostic or suggestive of ACS? YES → Does the patient have typical or atypical angina pattern, radiation, diaphoresis, cardiac risk factors?
   - ST elevation → STEMI.
   - ST depression and/or T wave inversion → check cardiac markers (troponin, CK-MB) at baseline and repeat at 6 hrs:
     - Suggestive history, positive cardiac enzymes and ECG changes = NSTEMI.
     - Cardiac markers negative, new onset, crescendo or rest angina = unstable angina.
   - Pericarditis.
4. History and ECG suggestive of ACS? NO → X-ray chest or echo:
   - X-ray chest: area of lucency in lung parenchyma and chest wall → pneumothorax; infiltrate (with history and labs consistent with infection) → pneumonia.
   - Widened mediastinum (and history consistent with aortic dissection) and flap on echo → refer for dedicated imaging (CT aortogram): aortic dissection.
5. Assess risk for pulmonary embolism:
   - Low risk: send D-dimer, X-ray evaluation. Elevated D-dimer, or echo showing dilated RA/RV or McConnell sign → high risk.
   - High risk for pulmonary embolism (D-dimer elevated): refer for CT pulmonary angiogram to rule out PE.
6. If ECG, X-ray, cardiac markers and echo are normal: rule out other causes of chest pain based on history and available investigations. Patients with nonspecific chest pain, no ECG changes at presentation and at discharge from emergency, and normal cardiac enzymes can be discharged and followed up in OPD.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Visual Illustration for Acute Coronary Syndromes (ACS)
tables.caption: Visual illustration of acute coronary syndromes: clinical setting, ECG, troponin level and change, triage decision and diagnosis (from low to high probability of MI)
tables.content:
A chart running from LOW to HIGH probability of myocardial infarction:
I. Clinical setting, symptoms and vital signs: from localised chest discomfort (low) to widespread pain (higher) to cardiac arrest needing CPR/shock (high).
II. ECG: normal ECG → mild ST depression → ST depression → ST elevation.
III. Troponin level at 0 h: − (low); −/+; +; ++; +++ (high).
IV. Troponin change within 1, 2 or 3 h: −; −/+; +; ++; at the highest level, if any of the above, consider direct rule-in.
Triage decision:
- Troponin − at 0 h and no change: rule out MI.
- Troponin −/+ or +: observe.
- Troponin ++ or more, or ST elevation: rule in MI.
Diagnosis: rule-out → mostly noncardiac (some unstable angina or other cardiac); observe → unstable angina, other cardiac, or NSTEMI; rule-in → NSTEMI or STEMI (some other cardiac).

body.t:

- Target HR 50–60 bpm; avoid if decompensated HF, bradycardia, or high-degree AV block

- High-intensity: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg OR Rosuvastatin 20–40 mg

- Continuous telemetry ≥ 24h; watch for arrhythmias, AV block

- Daily weights; strict fluid balance

- Acute HF/Pulmonary edema: diuresis, afterload reduction, consider IABP
- Cardiogenic shock: vasopressors, mechanical support (IABP, Impella)
- Mechanical (papillary rupture, VSD, free wall rupture): urgent surgery
- Pericarditis / Dressler syndrome: NSAIDs, colchicine

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Algorithm for ACS Management > Step 6: discharge and secondary prevention
tables.caption: ACS management, step 6: discharge and secondary prevention (DAPT, medications, lifestyle, follow-up)

body.t:
- ASA 75–100 mg indefinitely
- P2Y12 (Ticagrelor or Clopidogrel) for 12 months post-ACS
- Consider extended DAPT (> 12 months) in high ischemic, low bleeding risk patients

- High-intensity statin therapy — lifelong
- ACEi or ARB — especially if EF ≤40%
- Beta-blocker — continue for minimum 3 years, indefinitely if reduced EF
- Aldosterone antagonist (Eplerenone/Spironolactone) if EF ≤35% + HF or DM
- SGLT2 inhibitor if DM or HFrEF for added cardioprotection

- Smoking cessation — most effective single intervention
- Mediterranean or DASH diet
- Moderate aerobic exercise 150 min/week after cardiac rehab clearance
- Weight management: target BMI 18.5–24.9
- Blood pressure control: target < 130/80 mmHg
- Diabetes management: HbA1c < 7% target

- Cardiac rehabilitation enrollment — strongly recommended for all ACS
- Cardiology follow-up within 1–2 weeks of discharge
- Repeat echo at 6–12 weeks if EF reduced or not assessed
- Assess for ICD if EF remains ≤35% after 3 months of optimal therapy
- Ongoing lipid and renal function monitoring

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Contraindications for Fibrinolytic Therapy
tables.caption: Contraindications for fibrinolytic therapy in STEMI: absolute and relative

body.t:
- Previous intra-cranial hemorrhage (ICH)
- Stroke of unknown origin at any time
- Ischemic stroke in the past 6 months
- Central nervous system damage
- Malignant intracranial neoplasm
- Other intracranial lesions (aneurysm or AV malformation)
- History of closed head or facial trauma within 3 months
- Major trauma/surgery within the preceding 3 weeks
- Suspected aortic dissection
- Active bleeding or known bleeding diathesis (excluding menses)
- Gastrointestinal bleeding within the past month
- Non-compressible punctures in [the past 24 hours]

- Previous ischemic stroke beyond 12 months
- Transient ischemic attack in the preceding 6 months
- Oral anticoagulation therapy
- Pregnancy or within 1 week postpartum
- Recent (2-4 weeks) internal bleeding
- Prolonged or traumatic CPR
- Active peptic ulcer (only if the ulcer is actively bleeding; if only stool occult blood positivity, may be considered for thrombolysis)
- Severe uncontrolled hypertension (SBP >180 mm Hg and/or DBP > 110 mm Hg). Patients presenting with hypertension should be given beta-blockers, nitroglycerin and analgesics promptly to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of ICH following thrombolysis
- Patients on warfarin therapy have higher rates of hemorrhage: the higher the INR, the higher the risk
- Advanced liver disease
- Infective endocarditis

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Diagnosis of Stroke > Steps 1-2: recognise stroke and pre-hospital actions
tables.caption: Stroke, steps 1-2: recognise stroke (BE-FAST and additional symptoms) and EMS/pre-hospital actions

body.t:
- B — Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination
- E — Eyes: Sudden vision change (blurred, double, or loss of vision in one or both eyes)
- F — Face: Facial drooping or asymmetry — ask patient to smile
- A — Arms: Arm weakness or drift — ask patient to raise both arms
- S — Speech: Slurred, confused, or inability to speak or understand
- T — Time: Call emergency services IMMEDIATELY — note exact time of last known well (LKW)

- Sudden severe headache with no known cause ('thunderclap') — consider SAH
- Sudden confusion or altered level of consciousness
- Unilateral numbness or weakness (face, arm, or leg)
- Difficulty walking, dizziness, or loss of coordination
- Transient symptoms resolving < 24h = TIA — treat as emergency

- Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale (CPSS): Facial droop, arm drift, speech
- LAPSS or FAST-ED if available
- Blood glucose
- 12-lead ECG (rule out AF as cause, detect STEMI mimics)

- Airway: Protect airway; supplemental O2 only if SpO2 < 94%
- IV access × 2; NS (not dextrose unless hypoglycaemic)
- Position: HOB 0–15° unless airway concern
- Do NOT lower BP unless > 220/120 and clear hypertensive emergency
- NPO – aspiration risk

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Ischemic vs hemorrhagic stroke treatment
tables.caption: Acute treatment of ischaemic stroke (IV tPA/alteplase, contraindications, thrombectomy, antiplatelets) vs haemorrhagic stroke (ICH reversal of anticoagulation, BP control, surgery, SAH)

body.t:
IV tPA (Alteplase) — 0–4.5h window:
- 0.9 mg/kg IV (max 90 mg): 10% bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min
- Onset ≤ 4.5h from LKW (or wake-up stroke with DWI/FLAIR mismatch)
- BP must be < 185/110 before administration

Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH): reverse anticoagulation IMMEDIATELY
- Warfarin: Vitamin K 10 mg IV + 4-factor PCC (25–50 units/kg)
- DOAC: PCC or specific reversal agent (Idarucizumab for Dabigatran; Andexanet alfa for Xa inhibitors)
- Heparin: Protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 units UFH
- Antiplatelet reversal: Desmopressin 0.4 mcg/kg IV if urgent surgery

tPA absolute contraindications:
- Hemorrhage on CT or prior intracranial hemorrhage
- BP > 185/110 mmHg (uncontrolled after treatment)
- INR > 1.7, aPTT > 40s, platelets < 100,000
- Recent surgery/trauma < 14 days (serious), < 3 months (head/spine)
- Active internal bleeding
- Glucose < 50 or > 400 mg/dL
- NIHSS = 0 (resolved) or rapidly improving

BP control (ICH):
- Target SBP 130–150 mmHg within 1h of presentation
- IV Labetalol, Nicardipine, or Clevidipine infusion
- Avoid rapid drops > 90 mmHg in chronic hypertensives

Mechanical thrombectomy (LVO) — 0–24h:
- Confirmed LVO on CTA: ICA, M1, M2, basilar artery
- 0–6h: All eligible LVO patients (mRS 0–1 premorbid)
- 6–24h: DAWN / DEFUSE-3 criteria (CTP or MRI mismatch)
- Target door-to-puncture < 60 min; reperfusion < 90 min
- Alteplase + thrombectomy — do NOT delay tPA for thrombectomy

Surgical considerations:
- Neurosurgery consultation for all ICH
- Evacuation if: cerebellar hemorrhage > 3 cm, posterior fossa compression, obstructive hydrocephalus
- Lobar ICH > 30 mL with neurological deterioration
- EVD for hydrocephalus with impaired consciousness

Antiplatelet therapy (if tPA NOT given):
- Aspirin 325 mg PO within 24–48h of onset
- Dual antiplatelet (ASA + Clopidogrel 75 mg) for 21 days for minor stroke/high-risk TIA (NIHSS ≤3, ABCD² ≥4)

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH):
- 'Thunderclap' headache — worst of life
- CT head (90% sensitive within 6h); LP if CT negative
- CTA or DSA to identify aneurysm
- Nimodipine 60 mg PO q4h for 21 days (vasospasm prevention)
- Neurosurgical/Neurointerventional: coiling or clipping
- ICP management, euvolemia, avoid hyponatremia

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Step 3: ED arrival
tables.caption: Stroke, step 3: ED arrival, door-to-CT < 25 min (immediate actions, labs, imaging)

body.t:
- Activate Stroke Team / Neurology alert
- Rapid triage — priority 1
- IV access × 2, blood draws (see Labs below)
- 12-lead ECG, continuous cardiac monitoring
- Vitals: BP both arms, SpO2, temperature, glucose
- NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) assessment by trained provider

- Glucose (point-of-care STAT — must be done before tPA decision)
- CBC, BMP, coagulation (PT/INR/aPTT), type & screen
- Troponin, liver function tests
- Pregnancy test (women of childbearing age)
- Toxicology screen if altered consciousness

- Non-contrast CT head STAT — rule out hemorrhage
- CT Angiography (CTA) head + neck if tPA candidate or large vessel occlusion (LVO) suspected
- CT Perfusion (CTP) if extended window (6–24h) or uncertain onset
- MRI/DWI preferred if available and does not delay tPA; better for posterior fossa

tables.context_before: Arrange brain CT < 1 hour of arrival. Use the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) to stratify the severity of stroke: score < 6 mild stroke; 6-24 moderate to severe stroke; >25 severe stroke.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Step 4: acute stroke unit management
tables.caption: Stroke, step 4: acute stroke unit management for all stroke types (BP targets, glucose, temperature, airway, neuro monitoring, DVT prophylaxis, fluids)

body.t:
- Ischemic + tPA given: Maintain < 180/105 mmHg for ≥24h post-tPA
- Ischemic + NO tPA: Permissive hypertension; treat only if BP > 220/120 or end-organ damage
- ICH: Target SBP 130–150 mmHg
- SAH: Avoid hypotension; SBP 140–160 mmHg until aneurysm secured

- Target blood glucose 7.8–10.0 mmol/L
- Avoid hypoglycaemia < 3.3 mmol/L (worsens ischemic penumbra)
- Insulin infusion if persistent hyperglycaemia > 10.0 mmol/L

- Treat fever aggressively: target normothermia (< 37.5°C)
- Acetaminophen 650 mg q4–6h; cooling blankets if refractory
- Investigate source: aspiration pneumonia, UTI, DVT

- Supplemental O2 only if SpO2 < 94%
- Intubation if GCS ≤8, airway not protected, or respiratory failure
- Swallow evaluation before oral intake (bedside or formal SLP assessment)
- HOB 30–45° to reduce aspiration risk (except permissive hypotension phase)

- Neuro checks q1h for first 24h, then q4h if stable
- Repeat CT head at 24h post-tPA or if neurological deterioration
- Continuous EEG if seizure suspected or altered consciousness without clear cause
- ICP monitoring if cerebral edema, large infarct, or haemorrhagic transformation

- Pneumatic compression devices from admission (all stroke patients)
- Ischemic stroke: Add LMWH (Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily) after 48h if no haemorrhagic transformation
- ICH: Mechanical prophylaxis only for first 48–72h; LMWH after imaging confirms stability

- Normal saline (isotonic); avoid hypotonic fluids (worsen cerebral edema)
- Euvolemia — target CVP 8–12, avoid dehydration
- NPO if dysphagia; NG tube for medications and nutrition

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Step 5: secondary prevention and etiology workup
tables.caption: Stroke, step 5: secondary prevention and etiology workup (workup, antiplatelets, anticoagulation for AF, carotid disease, BP, lipids and lifestyle)

body.t:
- Prolonged cardiac monitoring ≥24h (preferably 72h) for paroxysmal AF detection
- Echocardiogram: Transthoracic (TTE) ± Transoesophageal (TEE) for cardioembolic source
- MRI brain with DWI for infarct characterization
- Carotid duplex ultrasound for ipsilateral carotid stenosis
- Fasting lipid panel, HbA1c, homocysteine if cryptogenic
- Hypercoagulable workup (young patients, cryptogenic): Factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid Ab, Protein C/S
- TOAST classification: Large artery, Cardioembolic, Small vessel, Other, Cryptogenic

- Minor stroke/TIA: DAPT (ASA 81 mg + Clopidogrel 75 mg) × 21 days, then monotherapy
- Moderate-severe stroke: ASA 81 mg monotherapy (or Clopidogrel if ASA-intolerant)
- Do NOT use DAPT long-term (> 3 months) — increases bleeding risk without benefit

- AF-related stroke: Start DOAC 3–14 days after stroke (1–2 weeks for severe strokes)
- DOAC preferred over warfarin: Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran, or Edoxaban
- Cardioembolic (non-AF): Warfarin (INR 2–3) for mechanical valves; DOAC for others
- Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) + cryptogenic stroke < 60 years: Consider closure device

- Symptomatic stenosis 50–99%: Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) within 2 weeks of event
- Asymptomatic stenosis > 70%: CEA vs. CAS individualized decision
- Carotid artery stenting (CAS) alternative in high surgical-risk patients

- Long-term target: < 130/80 mmHg for most stroke patients
- Restart or initiate antihypertensive therapy 24–48h after acute phase
- Preferred agents: ACEi or ARB, Thiazide diuretics, or combination

- High-intensity statin: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg or Rosuvastatin 20–40 mg; target LDL < 70 mg/dL
- Smoking cessation — most impactful modifiable risk factor
- Diabetes management: HbA1c < 7%
- Mediterranean diet; limit alcohol; weight management
- Regular aerobic exercise 150 min/week after rehabilitation clearance

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Step 6: rehabilitation and discharge planning
tables.caption: Stroke, step 6: rehabilitation and discharge planning (early rehab, rehab team, discharge planning, prognosis tools)

body.t:
- Mobilization within 24–48h of ischemic stroke if stable (avoid in severe stroke or ICH)
- Physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology — begin in acute phase
- Dysphagia screening before any oral intake; formal SLP evaluation if any concern
- Nutritional support: NG tube if oral intake unsafe; dietitian referral

- Physiatrist, PT, OT, SLP, neuropsychology, social work, case management
- Inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF) if patient can tolerate 3 hours therapy/day
- Skilled nursing facility (SNF) if medical needs require nursing oversight
- Home therapy if good function and support system

- Antiplatelet or anticoagulation medication reconciliation and education
- BP log; home BP monitoring device
- Fall risk assessment; assistive device provision
- Driving: Typically prohibited for 3–6 months; assess per local regulations
- Outpatient neurology follow-up within 2–4 weeks
- Stroke support groups and caregiver education

- mRS (Modified Rankin Scale) at discharge and 90-day follow-up
- Barthel Index for ADL independence
- NIHSS trajectory: improvement correlates with functional outcome

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Stroke management flowchart by facility level
tables.caption: Stroke management by facility level (primary clinic, health centre, regional/referral hospital) with key time targets and CT decision (flowchart)
tables.content:
Key time targets: door-to-CT < 25 minutes; door-to-needle (tPA) < 60 minutes; door-to-puncture (thrombectomy) < 60 min; tPA window ≤4.5 hours from last known well (LKW); thrombectomy window ≤24 hours (selected patients); CEA for TIA/minor stroke < 2 weeks.

1. Primary clinic: identify signs and symptoms of stroke (SPOT A STROKE: F face drooping on one side; A arm or leg weakness; S speech difficulty; T time to call for ambulance immediately). Take vital signs, check glucose level, support ABCs and give oxygen if available.
2. Health centre: take vital signs, support ABCs, and give oxygen if needed; establish time of symptom onset; check glucose level; transfer to hospital.
3. Regional and referral hospital: take vital signs, support ABCs, give oxygen if needed; obtain IV access, do FBC, U&E, PT & PTT, lipid profile, HbA1c and glycemia; treat hypo- and hyperglycemia (according to protocol); obtain a 12-lead ECG; emergent brain CT/MRI; assess stroke severity scales (NIH Stroke Scale or Canadian Neurological Scale); see neurologist.
4. Does CT/MRI show hemorrhage?
   - Hemorrhage: consult neurologist & neurosurgeon.
   - No hemorrhage: probable or confirmed acute ischemic stroke. Repeat brain CT/MRI if the first CT brain was negative:
     - Ischemic changes: confirmed ischemic stroke.
     - No ischemic changes: consider other plausible diagnoses.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Is the patient a candidate for thrombolytic therapy > rtPA eligibility criteria
tables.caption: rtPA (alteplase) eligibility criteria in acute ischaemic stroke: inclusion (all must be met) and exclusion (any = contraindicated)

body.t:
- Ischemic stroke diagnosed
- Onset < 4.5 hours
- Age 18–80 years old

- Acute/severe head trauma within 3 months
- Ischemic stroke within 3 months
- Previous ICH
- Suspected SAH
- Intracerebral tumor
- Intracranial/intraspinal surgery within 3 months
- Active internal bleeding
- GI malignancy or serious GI bleed within 3 months
- Extensive hypoattenuation or hemorrhage on CT
- Known bleeding diathesis
- Aortic dissection
- Infective endocarditis
- Recent myocardial infarction
- Heparin within 48h (APTT prolonged) or LMWH within 24h
- Direct thrombin or factor Xa inhibitor within 48h
- NIHSS < 6 or > 25
- BP > 185/110 mmHg
- Platelets < 100,000/mm³
- Glucose > 22.2 mmol/L or < 2.7 mmol/L

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Is the patient a candidate for thrombolytic therapy > Acute management, contraindications and secondary prevention
tables.caption: Acute ischaemic stroke: acute management (alteplase, labetalol, thrombectomy, cerebral oedema), thrombolysis contraindications (absolute and relative), and secondary stroke prevention

body.t:
1. IV Alteplase (0.9 mg/kg: 10% bolus in 1 min, rest over 1 hour) given if 3-4.5 hours from stroke symptom onset. No anticoagulation or antiplatelets within 24h of lysis.
2. IV labetalol if SBP > 220 mmHg or DBP > 120 mmHg, or active ischemic coronary heart disease, heart failure, aortic dissection, hypertensive encephalopathy, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia: 15% lowering during the first 24 h; if lysis, keep BP < 180/105 mmHg.
3. Endovascular thrombectomy.
4. Cerebral edema: HOB > 30°, IV mannitol, or hemicraniectomy.

1. Any prior ICH
2. Intracranial neoplasm, aneurysm, AVM
3. Ischemic stroke within 3 months, 2 months' head/spine surgery
4. Bleeding diathesis
5. Suspected aortic dissection
6. Severe uncontrolled HTN

1. Severe HTN SBP > 180 or DBP > 110 mmHg
2. Ischemic stroke > 3 months
3. CPR > 10 min, trauma/major surgery within 3 weeks
4. Internal bleed within 2-4 weeks, active PUD
5. Pregnancy
6. Non-compressible vascular punctures
7. Platelets < 100k, INR [>] 1.7, PTT > 40, glycemia < 50 mg/dl

1. Antiplatelets: ASA 100 mg OD
2. Anticoagulants: consider in AF (CHA2DS2-VASc score), cardiac and paradoxical emboli (except endocarditis), hypercoagulable state; e.g. NOACs (rivaroxaban 20 mg OD) or warfarin (INR 2-3)
3. Statin: atorvastatin 40-80 mg OD, or rosuvastatin 20 mg OD (for life)
4. Blood pressure reduction (24-48 h after stroke onset; goal blood pressure '< 130/< 180' as printed; see Hypertension protocol)
5. Carotid revascularization
6. DVT prophylaxis: SC Lovenox (enoxaparin) 40 mg OD
7. Lifestyle modification: smoking cessation, management of obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, alcohol moderation/cessation

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Rheumatic Fever > Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF)
tables.caption: Diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever by the revised Jones criteria (2015): major and minor manifestations, evidence of preceding GAS infection, and diagnostic rules
tables.content:
Diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) by the revised Jones criteria (2015):
- Major manifestations: carditis (clinical/subclinical); polyarthritis/migratory arthritis; Sydenham's chorea; erythema marginatum.
- Minor manifestations: 1. fever (≥38°C); 2. monoarthralgia; 3. prolonged PR interval on ECG; 4. increased acute phase reactants (ESR ≥30 mm/hour or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dl).
- Evidence of preceding GAS infection: 1. GAS on throat swab (positive culture); 2. raised ASO titre; 3. raised anti-DNase B; 4. positive quick strep test.

The diagnosis of ARF is confirmed in any of these situations:
1. Two major manifestations and any evidence of preceding GAS infection, OR
2. One major and two minor manifestations and any evidence of preceding GAS infection, OR
3. Presence of rheumatic chorea.
source_flags: Subcutaneous nodules are a major manifestation in the text above (item 4) but are missing from the major list in this chart.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Rheumatic Heart Disease > Diagnostic findings according to diagnostic modality
tables.caption: Rheumatic heart disease: chest X-ray and ECG findings by valvular lesion (mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation)

body.t:
- Straightening of left heart border
- Double right heart border
- Splaying of carina
- Pulmonary venous congestion (e.g., Kerley B lines, bat wings)

- P mitrale (broad, notched P wave in lead II)
- Atrial fibrillation (AF) common

- Enlarged left atrium (LA) and left ventricle (LV)
- Pulmonary venous congestion

- Features of LA and LV enlargement
- Atrial fibrillation may be present

- Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)
- ± T-wave inversion in V6

- LV-type cardiomegaly
- Features of pulmonary venous hypertension

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Rheumatic Heart Disease > Algorithm with the Initial Evaluation and Management of RHD in Children
tables.caption: Initial evaluation and management of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease in children (algorithm: Jones criteria, primary and secondary penicillin prophylaxis by weight, valve involvement)
tables.content:
Acute rheumatic fever (ARF):
- 2-4 weeks after Group A Streptococcus. Diagnosis based on the revised Jones criteria:
  - Major manifestations: pancarditis; subcutaneous nodules; Sydenham chorea; erythema marginatum; arthritis (usually migratory polyarthritis).
  - Minor manifestations: fever 38°C; prolonged PR interval (on ECG); ESR 60 mm in the first hour and/or CRP 3.0 mg/dL; arthralgia.
  - Diagnosis, initial ARF: 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor. Recurrent ARF: criteria for initial ARF OR 3 minor.
- Management:
  - Primary prevention: penicillin V. If <27 kg: 250 mg 2 to 3 times daily for 10 days. If >27 kg: 500 mg 2 to 3 times daily for 10 days.
  - Secondary prevention: Extencilline (benzathine penicillin G), as printed: 'If >27 kg: 600,000 IU IM single dose every 28 days'; 'If >27 kg: 1.2M IU IM single dose every 28 days'.
  - If allergic to penicillins: azithromycin 6 mg/kg/day, maximum dose 250 mg.
  - Supportive treatment: arthritis, >2 years old: ibuprofen PO 10 to 20 mg/kg/day every 12 hours (maximum daily dose 1000 mg).

Rheumatic heart disease (RHD): still prevalent in resource-limited settings; sequela of untreated ARF; definitive diagnosis by echocardiography. By valve:
- Mitral valve involvement (most common): mitral regurgitation/mitral stenosis. Presentation: dyspnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, systolic murmur at the apex, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- Aortic valve involvement (commonly with mitral valve): aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis. Presentation: wide pulse pressure, syncope, thrill, diastolic/systolic (AR/AS) murmur, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- Tricuspid valve involvement (less common, very rarely isolated). Presentation: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, systolic murmur at the LLSB, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- For every valve: secondary prevention with Extencilline: if <27 kg 600,000 IU IM single dose every 28 days; if >27 kg 1.2M IU IM single dose every 28 days (the mitral column prints 'If <27 kg: 1.2M IU'). Treat heart failure as in the HF algorithm. A paediatric cardiologist decides the indication and timing of cardiac surgery.

*To prevent pain from the Extencilline injection, mix the drug with low-dose lidocaine hydrochloride 1% (3.5-5 mls) solution.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Rheumatic Heart Disease > Algorithm for Management of Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) at Secondary Care Level
tables.caption: Management of rheumatic heart disease at secondary care level (algorithm by valve lesion: mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, aortic insufficiency, aortic stenosis)
tables.content:
1. Suspect RHD at the health centre if a patient presents with new onset dyspnoea, fatigue or palpitations, plus: fast and irregular pulse; hyperactive precordium; loud murmur; distended jugular veins; ankle/leg oedema.
2. Transfer to the district hospital: order CXR, FBC, RFTs, 12-lead ECG. Confirm the diagnosis with echocardiography.
3. By lesion:
   - Mitral stenosis (leaflet and sub-valvular thickening, commissural fusion, calcification and accelerated forward flow on colour Doppler; left atrium usually dilated): start PO atenolol 25 mg if HR >90 bpm and BP >90/60 mmHg; PO penicillin V 250 mg BID; check for AF to start warfarin 5 mg OD (therapeutic INR 2-3). If in pulmonary oedema, admit for IV furosemide. Early referral for balloon mitral valvotomy (BMV).
   - Mitral regurgitation (leaflet and sub-valvular thickening, restricted leaflet motion, accelerated backward flow on colour Doppler; LV dilation +/- dysfunction): EF <60%: treat per HFrEF protocol, add penicillin V 250 mg BID, urgent referral to a cardiologist. EF >60%: low-dose PO furosemide, penicillin V 250 mg BID, non-urgent referral to a cardiologist.
   - Aortic insufficiency (thickened cusps with rolled edges; accelerated backward flow on colour Doppler; usually with rheumatic mitral valve lesions; LV dilation +/- dysfunction): EF <60%: treat per HFrEF protocol, add penicillin V 250 mg BID, urgent referral to a cardiologist. EF >60%: low-dose PO furosemide, penicillin V 250 mg BID, non-urgent referral to a cardiologist.
   - Aortic stenosis (thickened cusps with rolled edges; accelerated forward flow on colour Doppler; usually with rheumatic mitral valve lesions): aortic stenosis is a surgical condition. Refer to a cardiologist to quantify severity and plan surgery. Avoid afterload reduction unless AI or MR is associated.

Please note: women should be educated and offered reproductive health services upon RHD diagnosis. Patients on warfarin should have their INR checked regularly and kept within the therapeutic range. Estimate RVSP by TR jet CW if it can inform management; check the tricuspid valve for rheumatic changes. Mixed mitral or aortic valve disease can be challenging for less experienced practitioners: consult for management. Secondary prophylaxis with penicillin is recommended until 40 years of age.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Congenital Heart Disease > Screening and Diagnosis > Congenital Heart Diseases Screening
tables.caption: Newborn pulse oximetry screening for congenital heart disease (flowchart: abnormal, indefinite, normal; repeat at 1 hour)
tables.content:
Measure O2 saturation in the right hand and any foot of all newborns between 24-36 hours of age.
- O2 sat <90% in the right hand or any foot = abnormal → screening failed: paediatric cardiologist consult.
- O2 sat 90-94% in the right hand and any foot, or >3% difference between right hand and any foot = indefinite → repeat measurements in 1 hour.
- O2 sat ≥95% in the right hand or any foot and ≤3% difference between right hand and any foot = normal → screening passed.
Second measurement (1 hour later): same three outcomes; indefinite → repeat measurements in 1 more hour.
Third measurement: O2 sat 90-94% or >3% difference = abnormal → screening failed (paediatric cardiologist consult); O2 sat ≥95% and ≤3% difference = normal → screening passed.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Congenital Heart Disease > Approach to suspected congenital heart disease
tables.caption: Approach to suspected congenital heart disease (decision tree: central cyanosis, hyperoxia test, acyanotic vs cyanotic CHD)
tables.content:
Suspect congenital heart disease with: blue since birth or soon after birth and persistently blue, worsened by crying; poor or intermittent feeding, excessive sweating during feeding, crying and sleeping; precordial bulge, exercise intolerance; recurrent lower respiratory tract infection; recurrent episodes of heart failure; squatting, cyanotic spells, loss of consciousness; chest pain, shortness of breath and palpitations at rest and on exertion.

Central cyanosis/hypoxia?
- No: acyanotic CHD → chest X-ray, ECG, echocardiography.
- Yes: cyanotic CHD or pulmonary disease; consider non-cardiac causes like sepsis. Do a hyperoxia test (formal or informal, 15 L of O2) and check O2 sat:
  - O2 sat rises (Yes): pulmonary disease / non-cardiac causes. N.B. the hyperoxia test is not definitive; it does not completely exclude CHD.
  - O2 sat does not rise (No): cyanotic CHD → chest X-ray, ECG, echocardiography.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Congenital Heart Disease > Acyanotic and cyanotic congenital heart disease
tables.caption: Acyanotic and cyanotic congenital heart disease: types, clinical features, imaging and management (pressure vs volume overload; decreased vs increased pulmonary blood flow)
tables.content:
ACYANOTIC CHD
A. Pressure overload (clinical manifestations depend on the severity of the obstruction):
- Pulmonary stenosis: If critical: ductal dependent; presents in the first days of life in shock. If non-critical: tachypnoea, poor weight gain, poor feeding, ejection murmur over the pulmonary area.
- Aortic stenosis: If critical: ductal dependent; presents in the first days of life in shock. If non-critical: tachypnoea, poor weight gain, poor feeding, ejection murmur over the pulmonary area.
- Coarctation of the aorta: If critical: ductal dependent; presents in the first days of life in shock. If non-critical: HTN in the upper limbs, radial-to-femoral pulse delay, systolic murmur radiating to the back.
B. Volume overload (clinical manifestations depend on the severity of the left-to-right shunt):
- ASD: asymptomatic; can present with recurrent chest infections and poor weight gain. Physical findings: no respiratory distress, ejection murmur (most of the time absent) at the pulmonary area, fixed split S2.
- VSD/AVSD: symptoms appear in the first weeks of life: diaphoresis, poor weight gain, poor feeding, tachypnoea, tachycardia. Physical findings: chest retraction, holosystolic murmur at the LLSB, hepatomegaly, Harrison sulcus.
- PDA/AOW: symptoms appear in the first weeks of life: diaphoresis, poor weight gain, poor feeding, tachypnoea, tachycardia. Physical findings: chest retraction, continuous murmur at the left infraclavicular area, hepatomegaly.
Management of acyanotic CHD: 1. General measures: nutritional support, prevention of URTI and infective endocarditis. 2. Medical treatment if in heart failure: Lasix (furosemide) 1-3 mg/kg/day; Aldactone (spironolactone) 1-3 mg/kg/day; captopril (with caution) 0.3-0.5 mg/kg/day. 3. Treat the underlying pathology surgically or by catheterization.

CYANOTIC CHD
A. Decreased pulmonary blood flow:
- Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF): clinical features depend on the severity of the RVOTO; tet spells, squatting, poor weight gain; cyanosis, SEM at the ULSB, no hepatomegaly. Imaging: chest X-ray normal heart size with a boot shape, oligaemic lungs; ECG: RAD, RAE, RVH. Management of tet spells: knee-chest position, oxygen, IV fluids 10-20 ml/kg NS, propranolol 0.1 mg/kg/dose. Definitive management: paediatric cardiologist decides the indication and timing of cardiac surgery.
- Tricuspid valve diseases: types: tricuspid atresia, tricuspid stenosis, Ebstein anomaly. Management: a paediatric cardiologist assesses the associated anomalies and recommends medical and surgical management.
- Pulmonary valve atresia: severe form of TOF; ductal dependent and/or with MAPCAs; early presentation, marked central cyanosis, single loud S2, continuous murmur radiating to the back and axillae; very challenging surgical management and poor outcome.
B. Increased pulmonary blood flow:
- TGA: often associated with other cardiac anomalies; early presentation, absent or mild respiratory distress disproportionate to the high level of cyanosis, absent or systolic murmur. Imaging: chest X-ray 'egg on a string' appearance; ECG often normal. Management: PGE1, balloon atrial septostomy, arterial switch.
- Truncus arteriosus: presentation in the first days of life, mild to moderate cyanosis, symptoms and signs of heart failure. Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings. Treat as in the HF algorithm. Surgical repair before PAH becomes irreversible.
- TAPVR: early presentation if obstructed, with severe respiratory distress, marked cyanosis and shock. If unobstructed: right HF symptoms and signs, fixed split S2, SEM at the ULSB, hepatomegaly. Treat as in the HF algorithm. Surgical repair when the patient is stable.
C. Others: HLHS, interrupted aortic arch, complex CHD; variable associated cardiac anomalies; symptoms depend on the pulmonary blood flow. If in HF, treat as in the HF algorithm. A paediatric cardiologist decides the indication and timing of cardiac surgery.

All suspected cases of CHD should be referred to a tertiary centre after proper counselling.

tables.caption: Atopic dermatitis (eczema): summary of patient management by severity (flowchart: mild vs moderate/severe, flare treatment, follow-up, hospitalisation)
tables.content:
1. Assess disease history, extent and severity, and the impact on the patient's and family's quality of life.
2. Educate the patient and carer about eczema care, trigger avoidance, and recognising and responding to eczema flares and infections.
3. Mild eczema: follow the eczema management plan: 1. daily bathing; 2. moisturiser applied top to toe at least twice per day; 3. trigger avoidance advice. Follow up within two weeks.
   - Improved: support optimal care at home, e.g. consider referral to community-based services.
   - Not improved: manage as moderate or severe eczema (step 4).
4. Moderate or severe eczema: assess for skin infections and compliance with correct eczema treatments.
   - Unwell or febrile: consider hospitalisation and/or IV antimicrobials.
   - Well: commence eczema flare treatment: increase moisturiser use to at least four times daily; eczema baths; topical steroids; wet dressings and compresses; commence oral antimicrobials if appropriate. Follow up within one week.

     - Not improved: consider hospitalisation and/or IV antimicrobials.

tables.caption: Hepatic encephalopathy: West Haven grading (unimpaired, grade 0-1 minimal/covert, grades 2-4) and management
tables.content:
West Haven grading, as summarised in the text:
- Grade 0: minimal, normal exam. Grade 1: mild confusion, sleep disturbance. Grade 2: lethargy, disorientation. Grade 3: somnolent but arousable. Grade 4: coma.

West Haven grading chart (beside the text):
- Unimpaired: 1. no signs or symptoms; 2. normal psychometric or neuropsychological tests.
- Grade 0-1: 1. also known as minimal or covert hepatic encephalopathy; 2. no overt clinical symptoms to mild decrease in attention span, awareness, altered sleep rhythm; 3. abnormal psychometric or neuropsychological tests.
- Grade 2: 1. obvious personality change, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis, dyspraxia, disoriented, lethargy; 2. objectively disoriented to time.
- Grade 3: 1. somnolence, gross disorientation, bizarre behaviour; 2. objectively disoriented to time and space.
- Grade 4: 1. coma.

Management: identify and treat precipitating factors (infection, GI bleed, constipation, drugs); lactulose orally or rectally (goal: 2-3 soft stools/day); rifaximin if recurrent; supportive care (hydration, nutrition).
Monitoring: mental status, electrolytes, renal function.
